en: Regarding the National Teacher Zhongfeng’s practice of "Binding the Mind to the Buddha" throughout the three periods of the day, a separate Dharma seat for the formal invitation is established. The head of the assembly strikes the *yin-qing* (guiding chime).
After the patron has offered incense and performed prostrations, the head of the assembly proceeds forward [followed by the Master], and the patron follows behind to the Buddha.
(The Former Master) offers incense.
The Rector recites the praise:
"The true incense of precepts and meditative concentration rises in flames, piercing the heavens. (The Lay Disciple) reverently burns it, releasing it into the golden censer; in an instant—

It billows and swirls, immediately filling the ten directions. This concludes the three recitations of "Yaśodharā Averts Calamity and Dispels Obstacles" (the Incense Cloud Canopy). Master Pi said: [End].
The ocean of awakening arises from the void; The karmic waves flow through this Sahā world. If a person reaches the other shore, In the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is a boat for returning home.

(Recite the Buddha’s name until the assembly stands still before the altar. Recite one scroll of the Heart Sūtra and the Rebirth Mantra three times. Upon completion, either chant praises or recite the following text.)
The Dharma King benefits all beings; his compassion and wisdom are vast and profound, pervading the ten directions without distinction between the hidden and the manifest.

Now, the斋主 (Zhai-zhu), [Name], respectfully requests the Venerable [Name] on the occasion of [Name]'s anniversary, specifically inviting this mountain monk to ascend the seat and, relying upon the teachings of the Dharma, perform the Buddha-recitation service for the three periods of the day.
Thus, may the deceased spirit, encountering such an auspicious opportunity, naturally maintain solemnity and dignity in their demeanor.
Please descend to this seat. We respectfully listen to the sublime Dharma and receive deliverance with single-minded devotion.

(The assembly recites the Buddha’s name; the presiding elder ascends the seat. Before the altar, one image of the Buddha Who Leads the Way is enshrined, and offerings of incense and flowers are presented. The *vinaya-dhara* intones the hymn:

As the incense in the burner is first lit, the entire Dharma-realm is suffused with its fragrance. All Buddhas in the ocean-like assemblies hear it from afar, as auspicious clouds form wherever it reaches.
As his sincere intention grows ever more earnest, the Buddhas manifest their entire bodies.
(Clouds gather; after three recitations are finished, the Master holds up the incense and says:
This single offering of incense has its roots coiled beyond the kalpas and its branches spread throughout the mundane world. It was not produced by heaven and earth; how could it—
Governed by Yin and Yang, the process of creation unfolds. I burn this incense within the burner, single-mindedly extending this offering to the eternally abiding Triple Gem,
the myriad spirits of the ocean of lands, and the Teacher of Sukhāvatī, Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Ocean—
all of whom we rely upon through this true incense, making offerings universally and in common.
(When the three recitations of the "Cloud Canopy of Incense" are finished, the Master and the assembly sit together below.
First Period:
Namo to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pond Assembly. (Recite this three times; this is raised by the Venerable Vinaya Master.)
The Buddha-spoken *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were great arhats, well-known to the multitude. Long...
The Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana,
Mahākauṣṭhila, Revata, Cūḍapanthaka, Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, Gavāmpati, Piṇḍola-bharadvāja, Kālodāyin, Mahākapphiṇa, and Bakula.
Rāhula, Ānanda, and other such great disciples, as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince, Ajita Bodhisattva, Gandhahasti Bodhisattva, and Nityodyukta Bodhisattva—
together with these and other great bodhisattvas, and Śakra Devendra and immeasurable devas.
The great assembly was gathered together. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra:

"From here, to the west, passing through a hundred trillion buddha-fields, there is a world named Sukhāvatī (Utmost Bliss). In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who currently dwells there, preaching the Dharma.
Śāriputra, for what reason is that land called 'Utmost Bliss'? Because the sentient beings in that country have no..."
It is free from suffering; because one experiences only various joys there, it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss, there are sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all made of the four jewels and surrounding [the land] on every side.
For this reason, that land is called Ultimate Bliss. Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss, there are ponds made of the seven jewels, possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
It is filled with water. The bottom of the pond is entirely covered with golden sand. The steps on its four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Above it are multi-storied pavilions, likewise adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, *vaiḍūrya*, red pearls, and agate.
The lotus flowers in the pond are as large as chariot wheels; some are blue with a blue luster, others yellow...
Yellow forms have yellow light; red forms have red light; white forms have white light—subtle, fragrant, and pure.
Śāriputra, the land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with such perfected merits. Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, celestial music constantly plays;
the ground is made of gold, and throughout the six periods of day and night, it rains *mandārava* flowers. The sentient beings of that land...
Every morning at dawn, they each take a robe-sack filled with various wonderful flowers to make offerings to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas in other directions.
Then, at the time for eating, they return to their own land to eat and practice walking meditation.
Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is thus adorned with such accomplished merits and graces. Furthermore, Śāriputra, that land constantly possesses all kinds of wondrous and marvelous things.
There were birds of variegated colors—white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śārikas, kalaviṅkas, and jīvañjīvakas.
All these various birds, during the six periods of day and night, produced harmonious and elegant sounds; those sounds expounded and elucidated the five faculties and the five powers.
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path—when the sentient beings of that land hear such sounds as these, they all bring to mind the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Śāriputra, do not think that these birds are actually born as a result of karmic retribution for their sins.
Why is this? In that buddha-land, there are no three evil realms. Śāriputra, in that buddha-land...
Furthermore, even the name of the evil realms does not exist there, let alone their actual presence.
All these various birds are transformations produced by Amitābha Buddha, intended to cause the sounds of the Dharma to circulate.

Śāriputra, when the gentle breeze blows through the rows of jeweled trees and the jeweled nets in that Buddha-land, they produce subtle and wondrous sounds, like a hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments.
They act simultaneously; those who hear this sound naturally give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha.
Śāriputra, that buddha-field is adorned with such accomplished merits. Śāriputra, what do you think?
For what reason is that buddha named Amitābha? Śāriputra, the light of that buddha is immeasurable.
He illumines the lands of the ten directions without any obstruction; for this reason, he is named Amitābha.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Buddha, as well as that of his people, is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas; therefore, he is named Amitāyus.
Śāriputra, since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed until now.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats;
they cannot be known by means of calculation. The assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise. Śāriputra, that Buddha’s land is thus perfected.
This is the adornment of merit. Furthermore, Śāriputra, those beings who are born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
Among them, there are many who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), so numerous that they cannot be known by calculation;
they can only be described as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). Śāriputra, when sentient beings hear—
Such a person should make a vow, wishing to be born in that land. Why is this? It is so that they may gather together in one place with such superior and virtuous people.
Śāriputra, it is not by means of few roots of goodness or causes and conditions of merit that one can be born in that land.
Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, hold fast to it...
If one holds the name for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days,
or seven days with a single mind and without distraction, then at the time of that person’s death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings,
will appear before them. At the moment of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land of Amitābha.
to the Land of Utmost Bliss in the world of Amitābha Buddha. Śāriputra, because I perceive these benefits, I speak these words:
if there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should resolve to be born in that land. Śāriputra, as I am now—
He praised the inconceivable merit and benefits of Amitābha Buddha.
In the east, there are also Buddhas such as Akṣobhya Buddha, Sumerukūṭa Buddha, Mahāsumeru Buddha, Sumeruprabhāsa Buddha, and Gadgadasvara Buddha;
Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges each, in their respective lands, extend their broad and long tongues, completely covering the three thousandfold world system.

In the thousandfold world-system, I speak these truthful words: "You sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Śāriputra, in the southern direction there are the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, the Buddha Yaśaḥprabha, the Buddha Mahārciskandha, the Buddha Merupradīpa, and the Buddha Anantavīrya. As...
These Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, each within their own land, extend their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and speak these words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sūtra on the Immeasurable Merit Praised by All Buddhas and Protected by Their Recollection. Śāriputra, in the western world, there is...
Amitāyus Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, Amitadhvaja Buddha, Mahāprabha Buddha, Mahārcis Buddha, Ratnākara Buddha,
and Viśuddhaprabha Buddha— these and other Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each from their respective lands,
extend their broad and long tongues until they completely cover the trichiliocosm, and speak these words of truth: "You sentient beings, you must believe!"
This is the *Sūtra Praising the Inconceivable Merit and Protected by All Buddhas*.

Śāriputra, in the worlds of the northern direction, there are Buddhas such as Flame-Shoulder Buddha, Most Victorious Sound Buddha, Unyielding Buddha, Sun-Born Buddha, and Net-Luminosity Buddha—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
Each, within their respective lands, extends the mark of the broad and long tongue, pervading...
It covered the three thousandfold great thousand-world system. He spoke these words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Śāriputra, in the world-systems below, there are the Buddhas Siṃha, Yaśas, Yaśottara, Dharma, Dharmadhvaja, and Dharmadhara.

In this manner, as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River each, from within their respective lands, extend their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and speak words of truth:
"O sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Śāriputra, in the world-systems above...

There is the Buddha Brahma-voice, the Buddha Constellation King, the Buddha Fragrant Superior, the Buddha Fragrant Light, the Buddha Great Flame Shoulder, the Buddha Adorned Body with Variegated Jewel Flowers,
the Buddha King of the Śāla Trees, the Buddha Jewel Flower Virtue, the Buddha Seeing All Meanings,
and the Buddha Like Mount Sumeru. Such Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each in their respective lands, extended their broad and long tongues.
[His] marks completely cover the trichiliocosm. He speaks words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sūtra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is it called the Sūtra Protected and Remembered by All Buddhas? Śāriputra, if...
If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, upon hearing this sutra, accept and uphold it,
or who hear the names of the Buddhas— all such sons and daughters of good family shall be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas,
and they shall all attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Therefore, Śāriputra, you all...
"You should believe and accept my words, as well as what has been spoken by all the Buddhas.

Śāriputra, if there are people who have already made a vow, are now making a vow, or will make a vow, desiring to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha—all such persons shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Whether they have already been born in that land, or..."
Whether in this life or in a future life— for this reason, Śāriputra, all sons and daughters of good family who possess faith should make a vow to be born in that land. Śāriputra,
just as I now praise the inconceivable merit of the Buddhas, so too do those Buddhas praise my own inconceivable merit.
And he spoke these words: "Śākyamuni Buddha is able to perform a most difficult and rare feat;

he is able, within the Sahā world-system, amidst the five turbidities of the evil age—the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life—[to manifest his enlightenment]."
I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, for the sake of all sentient beings, have preached this Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.
Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task:
having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I preach this Dharma that is difficult to believe for the sake of the entire world.

"This is most difficult. When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, accepted it with faith, prostrated, and departed.
The Dhāraṇī for Eradicating All Karmic Obstructions and Attaining Rebirth in the Pure Land,
Spoken by the Buddha Amitābha (Recite the Rebirth Mantra three times; recite three times at the Lotus Pond Assembly).
General Outline Why is this world called "Ultimate Bliss"? Simply because the myriad sufferings cannot invade it.
If a practitioner seeks the path home, They need only realize their own mind within the dust of the world.
Mind and mind are themselves Buddha; clarified butter, cream, and curd are all produced from milk. Buddha after Buddha is but mind; hairpins, bracelets, jars, and basins all emerge from gold.
A journey of ten trillion leagues does not separate east from west; within the twelve hours of the day, ordinary beings and sages share the same path.
Bowing the head with palms joined, the white jade brow-hair shines as bright as the stars; singing praises of the purple-gold countenance, it resounds like a crashing thunderclap.
The moon of purity is reflected in every body of water; the clouds of merit are borne by every mountain.

When the fragrant elephant crosses the river, a single invocation of his great name transcends the two deaths; when the kalaviṅka emerges from its shell, a thousand recitations of his auspicious title drown out all other sounds.
My humble sentiments can only conceive of this as inconceivable; yet with a single thought of turning the light back within, it is easy to proceed.
Ultimately, it does not dwell outside the mind; it is clearly right before one’s eyes. If this is truly so, then how shall we now, as the assembly, focus our mindfulness on Amitābha?

Regarding the three daily services of the Buddha, which do not involve the stages of realization or cultivation—how shall we proclaim that single phrase of personally receiving the prediction of enlightenment? (Strike the sounding block.)
The wind whistles through every tree with a thousand kinds of joy; Fragrance permeates every pond with four-colored blossoms.
(The Venerable Karmadāna raises his voice:
The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden in color; His marks and signs and radiant light are peerless.
The white curl of hair winds like five Mount Sumerus; The deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.
Within his light, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear, And the assembly of transformed Bodhisattvas is likewise boundless.
With forty-eight vows, he delivers all sentient beings, Causing those of the nine grades to all ascend to the other shore.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One.
(Recite the Buddha’s name one hundred times; the Venerable Leader then raises the hymn of praise.
The First Great Vow: Contemplating Amitābha, who delivers the Sahā world through his forty-eight vows, the nine grades of rebirth surge forth upon waves of golden light.
A jeweled net interlaces and spreads; may the deceased spirits be delivered from the river of craving (three recitations at the Lotus Pond Assembly).
Lecture: When striking the ruler, [it is said that] all sufferings arise from greed and desire; one does not know from where greed and desire arise.
Because one forgets the self-nature of Amitābha Buddha, distracted thoughts proliferating in all directions are entirely the teachings of Māra.
Birth is non-birth; the *dharmatā* is profoundly still. Non-birth is birth; the fruits of karma are manifest.
That which is called "birth" refers to the traces of the arising and ceasing of sentient beings. That which is called "non-birth" refers to the quiescent extinction of the Buddhas.

This is the very foundation. That which is the profound stillness of the *dharmatā* is numinous clarity and tranquil quiescence; it is primordially wondrous, truly constant, and not absent in any single thing.

It is inherently possessed by every person. Yet, because of initial non-awakening, the mind suddenly stirred; one took the false for the true, became deluded regarding oneself, and pursued external objects.
Consequently, one was entangled in the net of karma and transmigrated through the five destinies, constantly rising and sinking within birth and death throughout the ages.
From antiquity to the present, there has been no interval [in this truth]. One should know that arising arises from conditions, yet the *dharmatā* does not arise together with the conditions;
ceasing ceases from conditions, yet the *dharmatā* does not cease together with the conditions. Therefore it is said: "The *dharmatā* is profoundly still.
This is what is meant by "arising while being non-arising. As for "non-arising while arising," sentient beings enter the mind through delusion and confusion, accumulating karmic deeds.

The result is that one vainly undergoes the cycle of rebirth and falsely perceives arising and ceasing. Upon the essence of the *dharmatā*, it is like images appearing in a mirror or a jewel changing according to colors.

One should know that the light of the mirror is fundamentally pure and the substance of the jewel is free from blemish; while objects and environments manifest in mutual relation, they do not contradict the forms and images.
The coming and going of those forms and images is just like the solemnity of karmic results. Therefore, the Buddhas, regarding this solemnity...
Within arising and ceasing, one perceives only non-arising; sentient beings, within the profound stillness of non-arising, perceive only arising and ceasing.

This is solely due to the divergence between delusion and awakening, which leads to a lack of uniformity in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In reality, arising has no self-nature, and non-arising likewise has no self-nature.
Upon awakening, both arising and ceasing are non-arising; in delusion, even non-arising is arising and ceasing. Thus it is said:
Since there is nothing else apart from this, these are but one essence with different names.
If this is truly so, then Amitābha Buddha is my own mind, and my own mind is Amitābha Buddha. The Pure Land is this very world, and this world is the Pure Land.
Is it not simply that delusion and awakening differ? How could there be "saint" and "ordinary person," or "this side" and "that side"? Thus we know that [it is all] manifest...
The assembly before me: with the self-nature Amida and the tongue-faculties of the great multitude, they all turn [the wheel] together.
O virtuous ones, do you understand this fundamental Dharma-wheel thoroughly?
Arising and ceasing, non-arising and non-ceasing— In the Land of Bliss, who can restrain the actions of men?
Who knows that within ten-thousand-fathom red dust, The lotus flower blooms and the moon is perfectly bright?
(Recited by the Rector)
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, who possesses great kindness and great compassion.

(The Master and the assembly descend from their seats together and circumambulate while reciting the Buddha’s name one thousand times. Upon reaching the altar, they cease the recitation of the Buddha’s name and recite the names of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean Assembly three times each.
This being completed, they recite the Ten Great Vows: First: Paying Homage to All Buddhas. Second: Praising the Tathāgatas.
Third, extensively cultivating offerings; fourth, repenting of karmic obstructions;
fifth, rejoicing in merit; sixth, requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
seventh, requesting the Buddhas to remain in the world; eighth, constantly following and learning from the Buddhas.
Ninth, always acting in accordance with sentient beings; tenth, universally dedicating all merit to them:
"Sentient beings are boundless, I vow to deliver them; afflictions are inexhaustible, I vow to sever them;
Dharma gates are immeasurable, I vow to study them; the Buddha-way is unsurpassed, I vow to accomplish it."

Receiving praise, the Jewel of the Buddha is extolled without end. His merit was perfected throughout immeasurable kalpas; his majestic sixteen-foot body of purple-golden hue awakened to the Way at the peak of the Snowy Mountains.
From between his brows, the jade-white light radiates brilliantly, illuminating and dispelling the darkness and delusion of the six realms. At the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower tree—
May we meet and expound the true source of the Dharma.
(The Zen Master recites the Buddha’s name.
The sounding of the ruler is present within each person; Amitābha is inherently possessed by everyone. Within every heart, all is the Pure Land. When realized, it is everywhere.
Beholding the Buddha, one awakens to the realization that every step taken has been toward the West.
Thus far, we have established this Pure Land practice hall for the three periods of daily recitation; now, the first period of Buddhist rites has been completed.

May these aforementioned meritorious deeds be cast into the great ocean of Amitābha’s vows, solely for the sake of the deceased [Name], to ensure their rebirth in the Pure Land. We reflect that from beginningless time until this present life—
A single thought in opposition to the Truth causes the six sense-faculties to pursue delusion. Following one's emotions, one creates karma, even indulging in wrongdoing.
As for bodily actions, these consist of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; as for verbal transgressions, these include false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh words;

as for mental evils, one constantly gives rise to greed and anger, and deeply engenders ignorance and attachment. Due to these three types of karma, one is bound by the chains of illusory conditions, perpetually mired in the toil of worldly defilements. However...

Adrift in the vast expanse of time and years, wishing to seek liberation, we rely solely upon the power of repentance and cultivation to cause the transgressions of our eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind to vanish instantly at the thought, and to cause the fleeting defilements of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena to become pure immediately.
Furthermore, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss depends entirely upon the making of vows; we now request the assembly of Dharma practitioners to join in chorus.
[Recite] in unison. For the sake of the deceased, with a sincere heart, repent and make this vow:

All the various evil karmas created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, Produced by means of body, speech, and mind— I now seek repentance before the presence of the Buddhas.
Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them all. Afflictions are inexhaustible; I vow to sever them all.
Dharma gates are immeasurable; I vow to study them all. The Buddha-way is unsurpassed; I vow to accomplish it.
Namo Samantabhadra-rāja Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Recite three times).
The preceding confession and aspiration are hereby concluded (strike the ruler). The deceased [Name], you should know:
as for the teaching of the Pure Land, it relies upon the forty-eight great vows of profound compassion and mercy made by Amitābha Buddha.
By these powerful vows, all sentient beings throughout the ten directions are gathered; anyone who possesses faith shall attain rebirth there. As for "faith," it is the belief that [it exists].
In the Western Pure Land, one must believe in the matter of Amitābha Buddha’s gathering in of sentient beings. We sentient beings must believe that we possess the lot of rebirth there.
Although it is said that Amitābha gathers sentient beings for their rebirth, one must fundamentally believe that this is solely a manifestation according to one's own mind;
that through the mutual resonance of cause and response, it is ultimately not obtained from without. To believe in this way is...
This constitutes true faith. Yet, if one has faith but lacks practice, that faith will not be perfected. Regarding practice, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"If one completely gathers the six sense faculties and maintains pure mindfulness in succession, without relying on external expedients, the mind will spontaneously open. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"If there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, hold fast to it—whether for a single day..."

If for two days, or even up to seven days, one maintains single-mindedness without distraction, then at the time of that person’s death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, will appear before them.
At the moment of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
Such a practitioner is said to engage in the right practice; practicing thus, [one attains liberation].
If there is no vow, one’s practice will not be perfected. A vow must correspond with each of the forty-eight vows of Amitābha Buddha;
this constitutes the Great Vow. Faith, practice, and the vow—these three are like the three legs of a tripod; none may be lacking.
Now, you, the deceased spirit, should know that the single thought of the present moment is inherently perfect and eternal. Faith, practice, and the vow have always been your own self.
These inherent qualities have been possessed from the beginning; what occurs now is merely the manifestation of the radiance of the original nature.
Amitābha Buddha, the Unsurpassed King of Physicians, with his majestic golden countenance emitting rays of light from between his brows, serves as a compassionate vessel upon the sea of suffering.
The nine grades of the Lotus Land; may we together aspire to go to the West. (Lotus Pond Assembly: three recitations. First period of Buddhist service completed; descend from the seat. Second period:
(The Master and the assembly ascend the seat; the Ritual Master [Weina] raises his hand:
*Namo* to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pond Assembly. (Three recitations.)
The Amitābha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha (Recite the Amitābha Sūtra once in succession).
The Dhāraṇī for Eradicating the Root of All Karmic Obstacles and Attaining Birth in the Pure Land (Recite the Rebirth Mantra three times;
chant three times at the Lotus Pond Assembly). Ring the wooden clapper.
Having already attained Buddhahood this very morning, the Master who transforms the Land of Bliss has already deemed it too late;
how much more so for those who wish to go there? Take it for granted that by then the cycle of saṃsāra will have been exhausted.

Originally, throughout the ten directions, there is the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). Its mountain light and water colors are like space merging with space, pervading the entirety of the great [universe].
The earth is the homeland of pure tranquility; flowers smile and birds sing like mirrors reflecting mirrors. From this moment on, there is no returning; once you have returned, you have attained it.
Who can vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes? Golden arms hang down day and night, granted only to the traveler who alone receives them.
White jade hairs are never obscured by past or present; they rely entirely upon the aspirant to take them up. Thus it is said: "The myriad dharmas are..."
The light of the mind: all conditions are but the clarity of its nature; fundamentally, there is no person who is deluded or awakened. It simply requires realization this very day.
Now, for you members of the assembly present here, regarding the second period of Buddhist practice—how shall we bring forth the single phrase, "Simply realize it"? How shall we expound upon it?

Casting off all attachments, return and re-examine: the blossoming of flowers—red, white, blue, and yellow—is the Way within the Teaching.
Mind-only is the Buddha; likewise, mind-only is sentient beings. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
As for what is called "mind," there are many kinds. One is the "flesh-ball mind," which refers to that within one's present body.
That which is produced from the blood and vital energy of one's parents is called the "discriminating mind" (*citta*).

This refers to the various kinds of conceptual distinctions made upon present objects—whether good or evil, favorable or adverse. That which is called the "spiritual knowing mind" (*jñāna-citta*) blends with a thousand differences without becoming confused;

it passes through the three periods of time without shifting. It shines forth as a solitary illumination, standing apart and peerless. It does not increase in sages, nor does it decrease in ordinary beings.
[The waves] subside. A pearl alone shines amidst the dark waters of the life-and-death stream; the crescent moon of the *nirvāṇa* shore stands solitary and bright in the midst of heaven.
The Buddhas awaken to this and provisionally name it "mind-only. Sentient beings are deluded by it and thus give rise to false consciousness.

Therefore, the Buddha is identical to sentient beings, and sentient beings are identical to the Buddha. Furthermore, there is no Buddha apart from the mind, nor are there sentient beings; there is only delusion.
Because there is an interval between awakening [to this], ordinary beings and sages are vastly different. How could one know that the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—are without distinction?
Yongjia said: "In a dream, the six realms are vividly clear; upon waking, all is empty, and there is not even a great chiliocosm.
Since this is so, the Sutra says: "From here, to the west, passing through a hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī..."
Joyful! In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma. In essence, this does not transcend the Pure Land of the Mind-only;

it is the Maitreya (Amitābha) of one’s own original nature. By this one may know: for the deceased [Name] now present before us, their birth shall be amidst lotus blossoms blooming one after another, and their passing shall be amidst rows upon rows of walking trees.

Thus, we have circled through the various realms of existence and transmigrated through the four modes of birth. The ocean of karma is vast and boundless; the mountains of transgression are towering and precipitous. Were it not for relying on confession and disclosure, how could one ever escape?

Thus they were eliminated. Having finished the confession (*kṣamā*), they departed. They made a vow for the future, once again troubling the assembly of Dharma-practitioners. With a sincere heart, they confessed and made this vow:

I repent of all karmic obstacles arising from body, speech, and mind.

by means of this illumination, one sees clearly, and only then can the practitioner reach the objective realm. Therefore, one practices the recollection of the Buddha.
If such a person does not make a vow to be reborn there, even if they possess meritorious practices, these will be rendered in vain, for they do not accord with the Buddha’s intent.
You, deceased spirit, should now understand this meaning.

Ten myriad miles of sounding the *chī* do not separate one from the dust of the world; Cease regarding delusion and awakening as being distant or near.
In a single thought-moment, one exhaustively encompasses Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; this is precisely being a person within the Land of Lotus Flowers.

Facing the dust while turning one’s back on awakening, one plants thorns within the seven-jeweled groves; returning to the truth by abandoning delusion, one arrays pearl nets at the portals of the four modes of birth.
The myriad dharmas, whether horizontal or vertical, are perfectly enveloped within the One Mind. Beyond the realm of conceptual calculation lies Amitābha Buddha.
Severing the six sense-faculties, there is no time of contrived activity; in this land of pure tranquility, one traverses the eight directions at will.
It destroys the masses of darkness like the bright sun adorning the sky, and heals all ailments like the divine medicine Sudarśana. Thus it is said:
"A single recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha can extinguish the manifold sufferings of birth and death for eighty trillion kalpas. Such is its benefit—how could it be matched by mere analogy?
Can it be reached by words? It is just like this very moment of focused mindfulness. Regarding the third period of Buddhist activity, tell me:

"Even granting that it concerns events prior to the empty kalpa, the six-character Great Name ultimately encompasses them all.
An ancient said: "When a pure pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot but become clear;

when mindfulness of the Buddha is cast into a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot but become the Buddha. In the Western Heaven there is a treasure called the Pure Pearl; it is said that this pearl, when cast into [turbid water]...
If one places this pearl in turbid water, the water for the depth of one inch becomes clear as soon as the pearl enters it to that depth.
As the pearl descends from one inch to one foot, and eventually reaches the bottom, the turbid water likewise becomes limpid throughout.
One should know that the "clear pearl" is a metaphor for the pure mindfulness of recollecting the Buddha; the "turbid water" is a metaphor for the distracted and deluded mind.

At the moment when the deluded mind is in a state of confusion and disorder, if one can arouse a single thought and, as if facing the Compassionate Honored One, fix upon the six great characters of the name so that each syllable issues from the mouth and enters the ear, then this confusion will naturally become tranquil in accordance with that mindfulness.
From this single thought, one proceeds to ten thoughts, and eventually to every thought remaining unwavering; this is what is called "the characteristic of pure mindfulness" in the teachings.
This is the successor [to the Dharma]. Those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name must possess sincere faith and maintain a solemn and upright mind for the primary cause.
They should deeply reflect on the lamentable nature of the cycle of birth and death, and feel profound aversion toward the painful turmoil of worldly dust.

When they raise a single utterance of the Buddha’s name, there shall be no other views whatsoever; it is like the Great Sword of Tai-ā held level across the gateway, or like a great wheel of fire amidst the stars.
The surging flames blaze fiercely; when the myriad things encounter them, they are consumed, and upon touching them, they are injured.

Only when the mind is undistracted and both subject and object are forgotten does one reach the state of "arriving home"—a teaching that need not be reiterated, and a shortcut that requires no further mention.
This may truly be called the divine art of realized practice, the orthodox path that transcends expedient means, and the thunder that shatters the hibernation-chamber of birth and death.
Thunder! It is the sun and moon that illuminate the dark alleys of delusion. This evening, at the third watch, the rites for the recitation of the Buddha’s name shall be completed.
May the deceased [Name], by virtue of this supreme goodness, attain certain rebirth in the Pure Land. Now tell me:
before a single thought has yet arisen, does this very message still exist? *Strike the sounding block.*

By means of these causes and conditions of mindfulness of the Buddha, I shall enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows.
By virtue of the Buddha’s compassionate power, all transgressions are extinguished and roots of goodness increase. When the end of life approaches, one will know for oneself that the time has come;

the body will be free from the suffering of illness, the mind will be free from attachment, and the consciousness will not be inverted, as if entering a state of meditative concentration. The Buddhas and the assembly of sages...

Holding a golden platform in his hand, he comes to welcome me. In the space of a single thought-moment, I am reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Upon the blossoming of my lotus flower, I behold the Buddha;
I immediately hear the Buddha-vehicle and suddenly awaken to the Buddha-wisdom. Therein I shall extensively deliver sentient beings and fulfill my vow for Bodhi.

Responding to the various capacities of beings, you are worthy to serve as a lord of merit for humans and devas; you steadfastly maintain the precepts without transgression.

(Ascending the seat while reciting the Buddha’s name.
Since the recitation of the Buddha’s name arises from within the mind, how could the bonds of karma come from without? In an instant one turns one's back on the mind that recites the Buddha’s name;
in a single moment, one is again within the realm of karmic bondage. Now, therefore, let all of you rely upon the teachings and perform the three-period recitation of the Buddha’s name.

This matter is gathered as a supreme cause, solely for the sake of [Name], the deceased, to ensure their rebirth in the Pure Land. From this day forth, may the fragrance of their precepts be rich and pervasive.

The torch of wisdom blazes brilliantly; the clouds of delusion disperse, and the sky of one’s nature shines alone with clarity. As the dust of falsehood is exhausted, the ground of the mind becomes vast and unobstructed.

All faculties become perfectly pure, and the myriad karmas are suddenly emptied. With a single movement of thought, a flower blooms; gathering the dew and welcoming the breeze, its fragrance floats upon the jade pond.
With a single stir of emotion, a fruit ripens; enshrouded in mist and facing the sun, its reflection falls into the golden garden. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—

Abiding therein, one sports and roams at ease; this is not beyond one's capacity. One attains the enjoyment of Buddhahood, penetrates to the very source of the Dharma, and the constant light of quiescence manifests everywhere.
The great king of vows accords with every atom of dust. For the sake of the deceased spirits once more, I sincerely repent and make this vow.
All evil karma created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, Produced by body, speech, and mind— I confess all these roots of transgression.
I vow to liberate all sentient beings, who are of the nature of reality; I vow to sever all afflictions, which are of the nature of reality.
I vow to study the Dharma-gate of intrinsic nature; I vow to accomplish the Buddha-way of intrinsic nature.

The above constitutes the three periods of mindfulness. Through the vast and majestic name of Amitābha Buddha, endowed with myriad virtues, I exhort the deceased [Name] to repent.
May all karmic bonds and afflictions be eliminated. By making the vow to be reborn [in the Pure Land], one’s practice and vows become profound; thus, no merit shall be wasted.

We pray that the deceased spirits, upon hearing these essential teachings, will believe, accept, and practice them accordingly. From this moment, may they take up residence within the lotus womb, forever leave the ocean of karma, directly realize the stage of *avaivartika*, and bring supreme *bodhi* to full perfection.
Amitābha Buddha, King of Great Vows, whose compassion, joy, and equanimity are immeasurable, constantly emits white light from between his brows.
He delivers sentient beings to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where there are nine grades of lotuses in the pond of eight virtues and rows of wondrous trees made of the seven treasures.
If you proclaim the holy name of the Tathāgata, he will welcome and lead you to the West. If you chant the holy name of Amitābha, go together with him according to your vow.
In the western direction,
I dedicate all the merit of my boundless and supreme virtues and sublime practices;
may all sentient beings submerged in suffering swiftly proceed to the buddha-field of Amitābha.
To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, to all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā,
I take refuge in the Buddha. May all sentient beings perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all beings enter deeply into the treasury of the sutras, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
